nodes.label: The Government of India
nodes.full: The Raj in Calcutta and Bombay, which ran the Gulf as its western maritime frontier — the Bombay Marine, the Native Agents, the rupee — and whose strategic priority was to keep rival powers away from the approaches to India.
nodes.src: background — Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007).

nodes.label: The Saudi–Wahhabi state and Najd
nodes.full: The reformist emirate of central Arabia, whose first expansion reached Buraimi and aligned the Qawasim — a connection the 1819 British campaign was partly aimed at severing — and whose later revival kept pressure on the coast's hinterland.
nodes.src: background — Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880' (1968).

nodes.label: The Ottoman Empire
nodes.full: The power on the eastern Arabian mainland after 1871, holding al-Hasa and a garrison in Doha, and the rival whose claims the British treaty system was built to contain on the Qatar peninsula.
nodes.src: background — Anscombe, 'The Ottoman Gulf' (1997).

nodes.label: The pearl market at Bombay
nodes.full: The wholesale market where the Gulf's pearls were graded and sold on to Paris and beyond — the demand whose rise from the 1870s pulled the coast's whole economy toward the dive.
nodes.src: background — Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012).

nodes.label: The Political Resident and the treaty system
nodes.full: From 1820 the Government of India managed the Gulf's Arab coast through a Political Resident at Bushire and a growing network of Native Agents. Britain took charge of the shaykhdoms' relations with the sea and with each other, without formally annexing an inch — a paramountcy assembled treaty by treaty through the nineteenth century.
nodes.src: Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007); the Residency moved from Bushire to Bahrain in 1946.

nodes.label: Zayed bin Khalifa — 'Zayed the First' of Abu Dhabi
nodes.full: Zayed bin Khalifa took Abu Dhabi in 1855 and made it the strongest of the Trucial shaykhdoms — through the Liwa date gardens, the largest pearling fleet on the coast and control of the Buraimi oasis. By 1900 his authority was the benchmark of Al Nahyan power (his reign ran on to 1909).
nodes.src: Heard-Bey, 'From Trucial States to United Arab Emirates' (1982); Lorimer, 'Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf' (1908–15).

nodes.label: The Al Maktoum secession and Dubai's free port
nodes.full: In 1833 the Al Bu Falasah section of the Bani Yas broke away from Abu Dhabi under Maktoum bin Butti and settled Dubai Creek. In 1894 Shaikh Maktoum bin Hasher abolished commercial duties — the decision that made Dubai the coast's great trading port.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey (1982); the 1833 secession and the 1894 free-trade decree that drew merchants from Persian Lingeh.

nodes.label: Britain deposes the ruler of Bahrain
nodes.full: When Shaikh Muhammad bin Khalifa broke the maritime peace by attacking Qatar, the Royal Navy bombarded, deposed and exiled him, installing his brother Isa. It was the clearest demonstration that under the treaties Britain, not the ruling family, had the last word on the throne.
nodes.src: the 1868 events; the resulting recognition of the Al Thani in Qatar; Lorimer (1908–15); Onley (2007).

nodes.label: The Al Thani recognised in Qatar
nodes.full: Britain's 1868 dealings with Muhammad bin Thani, treating him as the man answerable for the Qatar coast, effectively founded Qatar as an entity separate from Bahrain. An Ottoman garrison then held Doha from 1871, and Qatar spent the rest of the century poised between the Ottoman claim and the British system.
nodes.src: Rahman, 'The Emergence of Qatar' (2005); the 1868 agreement and the 1916 treaty.

nodes.label: Mubarak the Great and the 1899 Kuwait agreement
nodes.full: Mubarak Al Sabah seized power in Kuwait in 1896 by killing his brothers, then — fearing Ottoman absorption and a foreign railway terminus on his bay — signed a secret agreement in 1899 placing Kuwait's foreign relations in British hands. It set Kuwait's course for the next sixty years.
nodes.src: Anscombe, 'The Ottoman Gulf' (1997); the secret Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement of 1899.

nodes.label: The shaykhdoms Britain recognised
nodes.full: From the 1820 treaty Britain dealt with the rulers of Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman and Umm al-Quwain as the responsible authorities of the coast. Ras al-Khaimah, demolished in 1819, was rebuilt under Qasimi rule; the roster of shaykhdoms that would one day federate was substantially fixed by 1900.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey (1982); the sequence of British recognition of the Trucial rulers.

nodes.label: The destruction of Ras al-Khaimah and the 1820 treaty
nodes.full: An East India Company expedition captured and demolished the Qawasim capital, then the shaykhs of the coast signed the General Maritime Treaty renouncing 'plunder and piracy' by sea. British sea power now underwrote the treaty order.
nodes.src: the 1819 campaign and the 1820 General Maritime Treaty (Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880', 1968).

nodes.label: The Qatar–Bahrain war and British intervention
nodes.full: A Bahraini and Abu Dhabi attack devastated Doha and Wakra; the Qataris retaliated at sea. Britain treated the whole affair as a breach of the maritime truce, punishing Bahrain and dealing separately with Qatar — the moment Qatar's separate identity was recognised.
nodes.src: Rahman, 'The Emergence of Qatar' (2005); the 1868 settlement.

nodes.label: The Battle of Al Wajbah
nodes.full: Shaikh Jassim bin Muhammad Al Thani's fighters ambushed and defeated an Ottoman punitive column sent from Doha. The victory, though it did not end the Ottoman garrison, is remembered as the founding assertion of Qatari self-rule.
nodes.src: the Battle of Al Wajbah, March 1893; Qatari national tradition; Rahman (2005).

nodes.label: The Ottoman occupation of al-Hasa and Qatar
nodes.full: Midhat Pasha, governor of Baghdad, sent an expedition that took the al-Hasa oasis from the Al Saud and pushed a garrison into Doha. For the next forty years the Ottomans claimed the eastern Arabian mainland, and the British and Ottoman spheres met, uneasily, on the Qatar peninsula.
nodes.src: Anscombe, 'The Ottoman Gulf' (1997); the 1871 Ottoman campaign into al-Hasa and Qatar.

nodes.label: From General Treaty to Perpetual Truce to Exclusive Agreement
nodes.full: The 1820 General Maritime Treaty banned war by sea; the 1835 truce, renewed until made perpetual in 1853, ended it for good — hence 'Trucial'; the 1892 Exclusive Agreements barred the rulers from ceding territory to, or dealing with, any power but Britain. The protectorate was built in three treaty steps.
nodes.src: texts in Aitchison, 'A Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads'; Kelly (1968); Onley (2007).

nodes.label: The anti-slave-trade engagements and manumission at the Agencies
nodes.full: Successive treaties — 1847, 1856, 1873 — bound the rulers to suppress the maritime slave trade, and an enslaved person who reached a British Agency could claim a manumission certificate. Enforcement in the nineteenth century was thin, and the trade in East Africans continued to feed the pearling fleets.
nodes.src: the 1847, 1856 and 1873 slave-trade engagements; Suzuki, 'Slave Trade Profiteers in the Western Indian Ocean' (2017); manumission at the Bahrain and Sharjah Agencies.

nodes.label: The Qawasim and the charge of piracy
nodes.full: The East India Company cast the Qawasim maritime confederation as the 'Pirate Coast' — a label modern scholarship disputes, reading the campaigns instead as the Company clearing a commercial rival allied to the Saudis. The 1820 treaty was written by the victor, and its language of 'plunder and piracy' framed the coast for a century.
nodes.src: Al-Qasimi, 'The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf' (1986); the counter-view in Davies, 'The Blood-Red Arab Flag' (1997); the 1820 General Maritime Treaty text.

nodes.label: The Shia communities of the treaty coast
nodes.full: Shia communities — the settled Baharna of Bahrain, the Persian 'Ajam' of the Trucial ports, the Hasawiyya — kept their own courts, mosques and mourning houses (ma'tams) under Sunni rulers and a British paramountcy that mostly left religious affairs alone.
nodes.src: Fuccaro, 'Histories of City and State in the Persian Gulf: Manama since 1800' (2009); the ma'tam institution.

nodes.label: The first Saudi reach into the Gulf
nodes.full: In the first Saudi expansion, Wahhabi authority extended over Buraimi and influenced the Qawasim, and it was the Saudi–Qasimi alignment that the 1819 British campaign was partly aimed at breaking. After the Egyptian destruction of the first Saudi state the reformist tide receded from the coast, leaving the older Maliki and Hanbali qadi tradition in place.
nodes.src: the first Saudi state's Gulf reach (Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880', 1968); the Buraimi Wahhabi presence.

nodes.label: The qadis and the majlis
nodes.full: Justice on the coast was administered by qadis applying Maliki or Hanbali law and by the ruler's own majlis for disputes and crimes. Religious learning was carried by a handful of scholarly families and by students who went to al-Hasa, Zubara or further afield; there were as yet no formal schools.
nodes.src: Lienhardt, 'Shaikhdoms of Eastern Arabia' (2001); the pre-oil legal and religious order of the coast.

nodes.label: The coral-and-gypsum wind-tower house
nodes.full: The pearling merchants built courtyard houses of coral stone and gypsum plaster, topped by wind-towers (barjeel) that funnelled the breeze down into the rooms. Muharraq and the Dubai Creekside quarter of Bastakiya preserve the finest surviving examples.
nodes.src: Bastakiya / Al Fahidi historical district, Dubai; the Bahrain Pearling Path (Muharraq), UNESCO World Heritage (2012); Coles & Jackson, 'Windtower' (2007).

nodes.label: Nabati poetry and the ruler-poets
nodes.full: The vernacular Nabati verse of the Gulf — recited at the majlis, exchanged between rulers, sung by the pearling crews — carried political argument, praise, satire and lament. Several shaykhs were accomplished poets in the form.
nodes.src: Sowayan, 'Nabati Poetry: The Oral Poetry of Arabia' (1985); the Gulf Nabati tradition.

nodes.label: Muharraq and the pearling town
nodes.full: The wealth of the pearl trade built dense merchant quarters of coral-stone houses, mosques and the pearl-dealers' offices (dukkans) around the harbours — Muharraq above all. The town plan itself, wound around the boat moorings and the merchant's majlis, is the pearl economy in built form.
nodes.src: the Bahrain Pearling Path, Muharraq (UNESCO World Heritage, 2012); Fuccaro, 'Histories of City and State in the Persian Gulf' (2009).

nodes.label: The Persian Gulf charted
nodes.full: Company survey officers — Brucks, Haines, Constable — mapped the Gulf's coasts, reefs and pearl banks in the decades after 1820, producing the charts and the 'Persian Gulf Pilot' that made the sea legible to outside navies and traders for the first time.
nodes.src: the Indian Navy surveys of the Gulf (1820s–1860s); the 'Persian Gulf Pilot' lineage; Brucks's 1829 memoir.

nodes.label: The coast in the European account
nodes.full: From the officers' narratives of the 1819 campaign to Palgrave's 1865 journey and Zwemer's missionary surveys, the nineteenth-century Gulf entered European letters as a coast of pearls, pirates and heat — a set of images that shaped policy and would take a century to complicate.
nodes.src: W. G. Palgrave, 'Narrative of a Year's Journey through Central and Eastern Arabia' (1865); the officer memoirs of the 1819 expedition.

nodes.label: Tribal genealogy and the oral chronicle
nodes.full: The coast's own record of itself was kept orally: the ansab (genealogies) that fixed a tribe's sections and alliances, the accounts of raids and pearling seasons, and the Nabati poems that carried political argument. It is the knowledge Lorimer's officers would later try to write down.
nodes.src: Sowayan, 'The Arabian Oral Historical Narrative' (1992); the ansab tradition of the Gulf tribes.

nodes.label: The nineteenth-century pearl trade
nodes.full: Pearling was the spine of the coast's economy long before the boom: a summer fleet of thousands of men, a merchant class that financed the boats and marketed the catch in Bombay, and a share system (the ghaws) that bound divers to their captains by debt. Rising demand from the 1870s began the climb toward the golden age.
nodes.src: Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012); Lorimer's retrospective pearling statistics; the ghaws share-and-debt system.

nodes.label: The dhow routes — Basra, Zanzibar, Malabar
nodes.full: Gulf dhows carried dates down to Zanzibar and the Swahili coast, brought back mangrove poles, ivory and enslaved people, ran rice and cloth from Malabar and Bombay, and dried fish and pearls to Basra. The coast lived by a seasonal, monsoon-timed carrying trade centuries old.
nodes.src: Sheriff, 'Dhow Cultures of the Indian Ocean' (2010); the date-and-mangrove trade with East Africa.

nodes.label: The date hinterland — Liwa, Buraimi and the bedouin
nodes.full: Behind the pearling ports lay the oases: the Liwa crescent and Buraimi, whose date gardens fed the coast and whose control was the basis of Abu Dhabi's strength, and the ranges of the bedouin who moved between well and coast with the pearling and date seasons.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey, 'From Trucial States to United Arab Emirates' (1982); the oasis–coast economic link.

nodes.label: The Indo-European telegraph down the Gulf
nodes.full: The line laid to carry messages between London and British India ran down the Gulf, with a cable along its bed. It was the first modern communications infrastructure the region had, and it tied the Gulf's tempo to imperial news.
nodes.src: the Indo-European Telegraph Department; the 1864 Gulf section (Bushire–Fao–Karachi).

nodes.label: The pearling dhow and the diver's gear
nodes.full: The sanbuk and the jalbut were built to the same sewn- and nailed-plank patterns for generations. The diver worked with a nose-clip of bone or horn, leather finger-caps, a stone weight to sink and a rope to be hauled up — a technology that had barely changed in a millennium and would not until the industry died.
nodes.src: Bowen, 'The Pearl Fisheries of the Persian Gulf' (1951); Agius, 'In the Wake of the Dhow' (2002).

nodes.label: Coral-stone building and the falaj
nodes.full: Coastal builders quarried beach-rock (farush) and burned coral and gypsum for plaster; inland, the aflaj of Buraimi and the Omani interior were maintained by their shareholders. Both were old technologies kept in continuous use — the material base of a society before cement, steel and the pump.
nodes.src: the farush-and-gypsum building tradition (Coles & Jackson, 'Windtower', 2007); Wilkinson, 'Water and Tribal Settlement in South-East Arabia' (1977).

nodes.label: The Gulf run from India
nodes.full: Through the nineteenth century the Gulf was managed by the Government of India, not the Foreign Office — its currency the Indian rupee, its Native Agents often Persian or Indian merchants, its naval force the Bombay Marine. Economically and administratively the Gulf was a western outwork of the Raj.
nodes.src: Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007); the transfer of Gulf responsibility to the Foreign Office in 1947.

nodes.label: Merchants across the water
nodes.full: The coast's commerce ran on cross-water communities: Indian (Banyan) traders and financiers at every port, Persian merchants at Sharjah and Lingeh, and Hawala Arabs who had themselves crossed from the Persian side generations before. The duty-free Arab shore was a magnet whenever Persia or the Ottomans tightened control.
nodes.src: the Banyan merchant communities of the Gulf (Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj', 2007); the Hawala.

nodes.label: The African and Baluch presence
nodes.full: Two other communities were woven into the coast by the sea trade: East Africans, brought as enslaved divers, servants and labourers, whose descendants became a permanent part of Gulf society; and Baluch from the Makran coast, who came as sailors, cultivators and — for the rulers — hired soldiers.
nodes.src: Hopper, 'Slaves of One Master' (2015); the Baluch of the Gulf coast (Peterson).

nodes.label: Keeping the rivals out
nodes.full: British Gulf policy through the century was defensive: keep the sea that was the western approach to India closed to rivals — first France, then Russia, then the Ottomans as they pushed down the mainland. The treaties with the shaykhs were the instruments of that exclusion, not an appetite for empire on the Arab coast.
nodes.src: Busch, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1894–1914' (1967); the Baghdad Railway question.

nodes.label: The scramble touches the Gulf
nodes.full: As European rivalry sharpened in the 1880s and 90s, French, Russian and German interest in Gulf coaling stations and concessions grew. Britain answered with a tightening ring of exclusive agreements — the Trucial Exclusive Agreements of 1892, the Kuwait agreement of 1899 — closing the coast to any other power just before the oil age.
nodes.src: Busch, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1894–1914' (1967); the 1892 and 1899 exclusive agreements as anti-rival instruments.

nodes.label: The diver and the debt bond
nodes.full: The diver borrowed from his captain to feed his family in the off-season and to fit out for the dive, and repaid from his share of a catch he did not price. Debts passed to sons. For most of the coast's men, life was organised around a pearling season that kept them permanently owing.
nodes.src: Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012); the salaf and khammas debt system; Lorimer on the divers' condition.

nodes.label: The enslaved on the pearl banks
nodes.full: A large share of the pearling workforce, and of domestic and dock labour, were enslaved people of East African origin. Some dived on their own account and bought their freedom; some fled to a British Agency for a manumission paper; most lived and died in bondage on the coast.
nodes.src: Hopper, 'Slaves of One Master: Globalization and Slavery in Arabia in the Age of Empire' (2015); the India Office manumission records.

nodes.label: The Ajam and the Hawala
nodes.full: The Persian-origin 'Ajam' of the Trucial ports — Sunni Bastakis and Shia Lingehis alike — became merchants, builders and craftsmen central to Dubai's growth, holding an identity poised between the Arab coast where they lived and the Persian one they came from.
nodes.src: Fuccaro, 'Histories of City and State in the Persian Gulf' (2009); the Ajam communities of Dubai and Sharjah.
